→ Restate the section’s thesis with memorable vocabulary: the upstream interface = the “fuzzy front end” of development (Zhang and Doll) — architect’s job there is to drive out as much ambiguity as possible, never “all of it” (Box 9.2)

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
What Is a PDP?



Nearly every large firm has a product development process (PDP) — capturing methodology, terminology, phases, milestones, and tasks/outputs.




A principal advantage: it’s a tool for reducing ambiguity by defining tasks and responsibilities
But it’s easy to be lulled into thinking the PDP resolves upstream ambiguity automatically — this is only partially true. A PDP can do the architect a disservice if it presumes more certainty than is actually present
We seek a PDP that is “birth to death” and “lust to dust” — capturing everything from first envisioning a product to retiring the last instance



Define the object of study: PDP = internal methodology nearly every large firm has — terminology, phases, milestones, tasks/outputs
Why it matters for an architect: principal advantage is reducing ambiguity by defining tasks/responsibilities — the Section 9.2 role, partially automated by process
Caution — easy trap: tempting to think a well-defined PDP resolves upstream ambiguity automatically — only partially true. A rigid-looking process with clean gates can create false confidence that strategy/market/needs/tech are well-understood when they’re still deeply ambiguous underneath
→ Ambitious target scope: “birth to death” and “lust to dust” — first envisioning through retirement of the last instance. Most real PDPs fall short; the four case studies (NASA, Helicopter Inc., Camera Co., Agile) each cover a different partial slice

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.1 · NASA’s PDP






Includes some of the fuzzy front end (feasibility, approval, requirements) and includes operations — since NASA is usually the operator of its own products. Very traceability- and review-heavy, reflecting low-volume, high-cost, high-perceived-risk systems. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.1.



First of four real-world PDP case studies — comparative frame for all four: what upstream/downstream activities does it include, what does that reveal about priorities?
NASA’s PDP (8 phases, feasibility → operations): includes some fuzzy front end (feasibility, approval, requirements as early phases); includes operations as an explicit final phase — NASA is usually the long-term operator of its own products
Conspicuously missing: upstream influences barely represented — just a single feasibility question where you’d expect rich market analysis. NASA’s “market analysis” is really budget decisions, public value, science goals, industrial base — not commercial market research. No explicit separate technology-development process shown
Heavy stage-gate/review emphasis (SRR, PDR, CDR…) reflects NASA’s reality: low-volume, extremely expensive space systems that can’t be tested in their actual operating environment first, high perceived cost of public (especially human spaceflight) failure
→ This traceability-heavy character has been both praised (enabled the celebrated Hubble mirror repair) and criticized (Columbia accident board questioned whether it surfaced known risks in time)

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.2 · Helicopter Inc.’s PDP






Compared to NASA, iteration loops stand out — even in aerospace, iteration is inevitable and not at odds with a stage-gated process. The process centers on FAA certification, itself an instrument of the more important process: sales. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.2.



Second case study — “Helicopter Inc.” (masked name): military/civilian helicopters, mostly government revenue, heavily regulated market
Compared to NASA’s clean, linear-looking process: explicit iteration loops stand out (dashed feedback arrows around detail design, fabrication/code, system testing)
→ Key observation: even in a NASA-like aerospace environment, iteration is inevitable and not at odds with an overall stage-gated process — the two coexist
Process’s real center of gravity = FAA certification — but push one level deeper: certification isn’t the goal, it’s an instrument of the more important process, sales (can’t legally sell/operate without it)
Open question the book poses: diagram includes product feedback but doesn’t show customers “up front” — does Helicopter Inc. conceive first then test in market, or gather needs first then design? From the diagram alone, customer input is present somewhere, folded into the mission statement, but its exact role/timing isn’t visible

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.3 · Camera Co.’s PDP



Camera Co.’s PDP explicitly shows upstream processes: strategy, voice of the customer, and R&D — all part of “conceiving”
Manufacturing process development precedes product development — Camera Co. is a process-driven industry
Raises a question: does the architect’s role in reducing manufacturing ambiguity matter more than innovation, given a stable customer base?






Third case study — “Camera Co.” (masked): film/cameras, amateur and professional
Contrast: explicitly shows upstream activities (business strategy, voice of customer, R&D) all folded into “conceiving” — unlike NASA’s/Helicopter Inc.’s under-represented upstream
Distinctive feature: manufacturing process development precedes product development — opposite of the default assumption. Camera Co. is a process-driven industry: how it can be manufactured shapes what gets designed
Discussion questions to pose:

Camera Co. is often seen as R&D-driven, yet voice-of-customer notionally precedes R&D/tech stream in this diagram — accurate, or aspirational (nudging a tech-focused company toward customer-driven)?
Market competition: distributed/diverse, unlike NASA’s unique-customer government relationship or Helicopter Inc.’s certification-gated market
→ Open question: given a stable, loyal customer base, is the architect’s role in reducing manufacturing-quality ambiguity more valuable here than driving innovation? No single right answer — the point is reasoning about what a PDP’s structure reveals about org priorities

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.4 · An Agile PDP






Agile emphasizes iterative, incremental development — collaborative teams evolve requirements and solutions evolutionarily. Originated in rapid prototyping of software for small/medium applications; since extended (with mixed success) to capital-intensive, longer-lifecycle industries. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.4.



Fourth and final case study — Agile — genuinely different philosophy, not just another industry’s flavor of stage-gates
Definition: iterative/incremental development, collaborative teams evolve requirements and solutions together, evolutionary rather than fully-specify-then-execute
Honest history: origins in rapid prototyping of software for small/medium applications, where iteration is cheap. Emphasizes close interaction among people building working code over heavy upfront docs/negotiation/planning (diagram’s overlapping developer/interaction-designer tracks)
→ Honest caveat: beyond software, Agile has been used — with mixed success — to “shake up” far more capital-intensive, longer-lifecycle industries, where its founding assumptions (cheap iteration, low cost of change) may not hold. Be an educated consumer: think critically about in what contexts Agile is appropriate, don’t assume software popularity transfers to aerospace hardware

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Comparing the Four PDPs
Are differences between PDPs superficial, or substantial? Some observed differences:

Existence/number of phases and phase exit criteria
Existence/number of design reviews, timing for committing capital
Requirements “enforcement,” degree of customer input/feedback/aftermarket integration
Degree of explicit/implicit iteration, amount of prototyping
Internal testing/validation effort, importance of traceability, timing of supplier involvement








Tip


Many factors could drive real differences: hardware vs. software, existing vs. new product, standalone vs. platform, production volume, capital intensity, technology push vs. market pull.






Step back and synthesize across all four case studies — the analytical move the book wants practiced, not just four admired diagrams
Central question: are the differences among these four PDPs superficial or substantial?
Observed differences: number/existence of phases + how rigorously exit criteria enforced; number of formal reviews + when capital commits; how strictly requirements are enforced + customer input/feedback/aftermarket integration; explicit vs. implicit iteration + prototyping amount; internal testing/validation effort, traceability importance, supplier-involvement timing
Deeper diagnostic question: what factors could drive real differences — hardware vs. software, existing vs. new product, standalone vs. platform, production volume, capital intensity, technology-push vs. market-pull
→ Book’s conclusion (next slide builds toward it): despite surface differences, there’s enormous common underlying structure — motivates building a single Generic PDP

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.5 · The Generic PDP






Four common activity groups: conceiving, designing, implementing, operating — a checklist, not a stage-gate process. The architect’s primary domain sits in “conceive,” but must move relevant downstream information back into the architecting phase. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.5.



Payoff of the comparative exercise — anchors the rest of the chapter
Despite real differences among the four case studies, there’s a large body of common effective practice — codified as the Generic PDP: four activity groups — conceiving, designing, implementing, operating
Crucial framing (stated at the top, worth repeating): this represents activities, not a sequence of stage-gates — NOT “first conceive, then design, then implement, then operate” in strict linear order (that’s the flawed linear representation the next slide criticizes)
What’s in each group:

Conceiving: strategy, functional strategies, customer needs, segments, competitors, technology, regulation, scope/plan, mission, conceptual design — driven by market needs and tech availability
Designing: preliminary/detailed design, requirements definition/elaboration, model development, flow-down, decomposition, interface control — converts concept into the info object defining what’s to be implemented
Implementing: sourcing, element creation, integration, testing, positioning, certification — converts design into reality; deliberately bundles software coding + hardware manufacturing + systems integration under one term
Operating: sales, distribution, logistics, support, maintenance/repair/overhaul, upgrades, product improvement, platform expansion, retirement

→ Visually important: “Primary Domain of the Architect” band sits under conceiving, but a “Downstream influences” arrow feeds back into it — architect must move relevant downstream info back into the conceiving phase, not architect in isolation (developed further in Ch. 10)

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Linear Representations Are Flawed



Studies have shown that linear representations of the design process are deeply flawed — they fail to represent iterations and feedback, presume a linear flow of time and effort across stages, and can mask a design’s immaturity when gate criteria are compromised.




The Generic PDP is a checklist of activities that appear in complete PDPs, not a mandated sequence
“Implementing” deliberately includes coding software, manufacturing hardware, and integrating into systems
“Operating” includes support and release of future product instances — ending in retirement



Why the Generic PDP was drawn this way: studies have shown linear design-process representations are deeply flawed (genuine research finding, not editorial opinion)
Three failure modes of linear diagrams:

Fail to represent iterations/feedback (the loops explicit in Helicopter Inc.’s PDP)
Presume a linear flow of time/effort across stages, when real projects rarely proceed cleanly
Most operationally dangerous: can mask a design’s immaturity when gate criteria are compromised — a project can nominally “pass” a gate on paper while the underlying work isn’t ready, with no visual signal

→ Restate intended use: the Generic PDP is a checklist of activities in complete PDPs, not a mandated order
Deliberate word choices: “implementing” bundles software coding + hardware manufacturing + systems integration under one term; “operating” includes ongoing support of existing instances and release of future ones, ending in retirement (“lust to dust”)

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Section 9.3.1 Summary

Nearly every large firm has an internal PDP — a tool for reducing ambiguity, but one that can mislead if it presumes more certainty than is actually present
Comparing PDPs across NASA, Helicopter Inc., Camera Co., and Agile reveals many superficial differences, but real underlying similarities
The Generic PDP codifies this common practice as four activity groups: conceive, design, implement, operate — deliberately not a stage-gate process



Checkpoint before the Global PDP — the chapter’s final major move
A PDP is a genuine but double-edged ambiguity-reduction tool: useful for defining tasks/responsibilities, dangerous for creating false confidence about how settled the upstream situation is
Students should name all four case studies and their distinguishing priorities: NASA (traceability/review-heavy, low-volume high-cost high-perceived-risk systems), Helicopter Inc. (iteration loops, certification-as-instrument-of-sales), Camera Co. (manufacturing precedes product development), Agile (iterative/incremental, low cost-of-change)
→ Hold onto the Generic PDP — conceive/design/implement/operate — as the unifying, non-sequential checklist underneath all four. Sets up the Global PDP

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Building the Global PDP

To further support comparison across PDPs, we construct an extended baseline: the Global PDP, in three nested views
Level 1 centers on the architecture of the product — function and form — as a reflection of product goals, themselves set to respond to market/stakeholder needs
The architect answers the canonical W Questions: why, what, how, where, when, who, how much








Tip


Quo is the shared Indo-European root of these words across languages — French qui/quoi/quand, Hindi kab/kya/kyon, and the seven circumstances of the ancient Greek rhetorician Hermagoras.






Chapter’s most ambitious construct: the Global PDP, three progressively broader nested views (this slide = Level 1; next two = Levels 2 and 3)
Level 1 centers on the product’s architecture — function and form (Ch. 2/4/5 vocabulary) — as a reflection of product goals, set in response to market/stakeholder needs
→ Architecture (form+function) sits at the literal center of the framework, since it’s what everything else exists to produce
“W Questions”: why, what, how, where, when, who, how much
Etymological color: all trace to Indo-European root quo — French (qui/quoi/quand/combien/ou/comment/pourquoi), Hindi (kab/kya/kyon/kitne/kisne/kahan)
Greek rhetorician Hermagoras: seven circumstances (quis, quid, quando, ubi, cur, quem ad modum, quibus adminiculis) = same who/what/when/where/why/how/by-what-means structure, ~2000 years ago
→ Implication: this cross-linguistic, cross-era recurrence signals the question set captures something fundamental about how humans interrogate any situation — an architect needs to understand all of these attributes well

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.6 · Level 1 — The Holistic Framework






Architecture — form and function — sits at the center of the framework. Interactions are two-directional; flow from left to right is not implied. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.6.



Direct visual realization of the W Questions — trace across the seven columns:

why → need/opportunity — the reason the system is built
what → goals/performance — what it accomplishes
how → function/interaction — how it acts
where → form/structure — the elements (form answers “where” because form exists and has location)
when → behavior/dynamics — when things occur
who → operator/user
how much → cost/expense

Two callouts head off wrong readings: interactions are two-directional (double-headed arrows); left-to-right column order does not imply flow direction — same non-sequential/checklist framing as the Generic PDP
→ Architecture (form=where + function=how) sits at the literal center, both geometrically and conceptually — everything else (need, goals, behavior, users, cost) surrounds and relates back to it

title: The Role of the Architect
section: Figure 9.7 · Level 2 — Design and Implementation in Parallel
text:
Figure 9.7 · Level 2 — Design and Implementation in Parallel






Moving up a layer: the design process and implementation process each get their own instantiation of the W Questions. The design process has its own form too — notably design tools, which shape and constrain the system form that’s achievable. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.7.



Level 2: adds two more full applications of the same seven W Questions — one for the design process, one for the implementation process — running in parallel alongside Level 1’s “conceiving” row (three horizontal rows: Design process / Conceiving the product and operations / Implement process)
Subtle key point: the design process is itself a system with its own form — notably design tools. A straightedge vs. a French curve produces different renderings, hence different achievable system forms — the tools used to design meaningfully constrain what’s achievable
Automotive example: many automakers split non-recurring engineering (NRE) design costs evenly across platform variants launched the same year/volume — not part of any technical evaluation, wouldn’t show up in a stage-gate review, but clearly part of the Generic/Global PDP because it materially affects whether a variant can economically deliver value
Implementation process similarly has its own capabilities/limitations the architect must factor in — existing manufacturing/coding capability constrains what can be built regardless of the paper design
→ Practical use: critically evaluate any PDP or new design method against the 21 implicit questions (3 rows × 7 W Questions) — few methods answer all 21; the value is seeing which areas a framework is strongest in. Example: Lean began from Toyota Production System studies (manufacturing cost/quality), moved upstream to design-for-lean-manufacturing, and (more controversially) has also been applied to the design process itself — far removed from Lean’s original intent

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.8 · Level 3 — The Enterprise Context






The broadest nested view: the firm’s PDP inside the enterprise boundary (R&D and corporate functions mostly upstream; PR, sales, distribution mostly downstream), plus external actors and attributes — capital, competition, regulation — that affect the enterprise. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.8.



Level 3, the broadest view: whole PDP (conceive/design/implement/operate, overlapping ellipses, architecture at the center intersection) placed inside a larger enterprise boundary
Firm functions positioned by upstream/downstream role: R&D and corporate functions primarily upstream (feed conceiving); PR/sales/distribution primarily downstream (connected to operating); some (human skills, information systems, engineering tools) permeate the whole diagram; others (corporate strategy) play multiple roles at once
Outside the enterprise boundary: an explicitly incomplete list of external actors/attributes — capital availability, competition intensity, social impact — shown as inputs/outputs crossing the boundary

In: global economy, shareholder goals, political inputs, human resources, regulations, customer needs, competition, technology, services, raw material
Out: economic impact, profits, political impact, social impact, corporate image, IP, goods, services, technology, pollution

→ Purpose of this broadest view (easy to misread as detail-for-its-own-sake): reminds the architect that understanding the PDP’s contents alone isn’t sufficient — must also track issues influencing the firm and its context (Box 9.3 next)

title: The Role of the Architect
section: Box 9.3 · Principle of the Stress of Modern Practice
text:
Box 9.3 · Principle of the Stress of Modern Practice



“Things which matter most must never be at the mercy of things which matter least.” — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe



Modern product development — with concurrency, distributed teams, and early supplier engagement — places even more emphasis on having a good architecture:

Accelerating development via concurrency increases the importance of initial conceptual decisions
Empowering distributed/non-collocated teams increases the importance of well-coordinated, visible high-level design guidance
Involving suppliers early increases the importance of an architectural concept and baseline — suppliers can define or defy decomposition



Close the Global PDP discussion — Goethe quote (“things which matter most must never be at the mercy of things which matter least”) captures the worry: modern pressures can let minor operational details crowd out consequential early architectural decisions
Each modern trend raises the stakes on getting architecture right, not lowers them (contrary to a naive “efficiency improvement” reading):

Concurrency: parallel activities lock in initial conceptual decisions faster, less room to course-correct — getting them right upfront matters more
Distributed/non-collocated teams: well-coordinated, visible high-level design guidance matters more — without it, autonomous teams drift out of alignment
Early supplier engagement: architectural concept/baseline matters more — suppliers can either define or defy the intended decomposition depending on how clearly it’s communicated

→ Overarching message: none of these three practices are inherently bad — but each raises the cost of not having architected well, which is why this principle closes the chapter

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Section 9.3.2 Summary

The Global PDP is a nested framework used to compare different PDPs on a common baseline, built around the canonical W Questions
It reveals the architect’s system boundary — largely, but not exclusively, the “conceive” activities
The purpose of the broadest view is to remind the architect: understanding the contents of the PDP is not sufficient — the firm and its context matter too



Closing checkpoint for the whole PDP discussion — students should describe all three nested levels in order: product architecture (center), design/implementation processes in parallel (own W Questions, own form — design tools), whole enterprise context (upstream/downstream functions + external actors)
Built specifically to give a common baseline for comparing genuinely different PDPs (NASA, Helicopter Inc., Camera Co., Agile) fairly, not superficially
Concrete takeaway: architect’s primary system boundary is largely (not exclusively) the “conceive” activities — with the caveat (Fig. 9.5) that downstream info must still be actively moved back in
→ Broadest lesson: understanding PDP contents alone is necessary but not sufficient — firm and context matter too. Transitions into the civil-architecture case study, where “context” is nearly sacred

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Where “Architect” Comes From
By Steve Imrich, Architect and Principal at Cambridge Seven Associates

Civil architecture has an interpretive-interactive-performance aspect that differs from most industrial/product design — buildings inherit complex cultural and symbolic qualities affecting space, materials, and user experience
Ideally, the “special problems” of a building inform its design — as with helicopters, sailboats, or computers, concept/design/engineering can transcend mere style
Because buildings are only seen/experienced as part of their site, their special problems always relate to a wider context: time, culture, infrastructure, human behavior, environment, re-interpreted use
Buildings are rarely mocked up beforehand — a large element of risk, usually associated with the arts



Closing case study, unusual format: guest contribution by practicing civil architect Steve Imrich (Cambridge Seven Associates) — included because the word “architect” is borrowed directly from civil/building architecture, worth hearing from the original field
Central question to pose: what do civil architecture and system architecture actually share?
Distinguishing feature #1: buildings carry an interpretive-interactive-performance aspect more pronounced than most product design — inherit complex cultural/symbolic qualities affecting space, materials, user experience beyond pure function
“Special problems” (recurring phrase): a building’s special problems — particular, non-generic challenges of that site/client/moment — should inform its design

Parallel to other fields: helicopters, sailboats, computers successfully resolve their own special problems, where concept+design+engineering transcend mere style — callback to the Principle of Elegance (Ch. 13)

Two more distinguishing features: buildings are only seen/experienced as part of their site, so special problems always relate to a wide context (time, culture, infrastructure, human behavior, environment, re-interpreted use)
→ Buildings are rarely mocked up beforehand — a large element of risk, one the book says is generally associated more with the arts than conventional engineering

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.9 · Concept in Civil Architecture






Left: Trulli houses, Alberobello, Italy (a). Right: industrial ductwork, Centre Pompidou, Paris (b). The concept is the departure point for integrating performance and form. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.9. Photos: (a) Funkyfood London-Paul Williams/Alamy, (b) Francisco Javier Gil/Fotolia.



Contrasting image pair makes “concept” concrete in civil architecture, extending Ch. 7’s concept vocabulary
Trulli houses (Alberobello, Italy) — conical stone roofs — vs. Centre Pompidou (Paris) — exposes structural/mechanical systems on the exterior. Stylistically opposite, same underlying idea: the concept is the departure point for integrating performance and form
Preview: next slide’s six “design process with attitude” ideas (context, content, concept, circuitry, character, magic) — concept is one of two the guest author focuses on most deeply (the other: magic, a few slides later)
→ Precise definition: concept = departure point for organization/experience, the unifying idea by which all design decisions get evaluated. Conical roofs responding to climate, or a museum making its mechanical guts a visual statement — either way, one strong organizing idea lets performance and form cohere (same pattern as Ch. 2’s process/operand, instrument/process/operand)

title: The Role of the Architect
section: Six Ideas in “Design Process with Attitude”
text:
Six Ideas in “Design Process with Attitude”

Context — the built environment, cultural norms, and history of the organizations and people the building serves
Content — the building’s programmatic requirements and functional performance
Concept — the unifying idea by which all design decisions are evaluated; concept generation succeeds when it integrates and balances the nature of content and context
Circuitry — the connective tissue between functional components; more than a path from A to B, it creates interest and anticipation
Character — a building’s material, site, and sense of life beyond the aggregation of parts
Magic — the largely intangible quality defined by the user’s experience; magic fosters delight and joyful appreciation of the unexpected



Guest author’s vocabulary — “design process with attitude”, deliberately contrasted against a conventional PDP. Define each of the six:

Context: the wider setting — adjacent buildings, cultural norms, environmental conditions, history/motivations of the people the building serves
Content: what the building is for — programmatic requirements + functional performance (Ch. 5’s function vocabulary, at building scale)
Concept: the unifying idea all decisions are evaluated by — succeeds specifically when it integrates and balances content and context together
Circuitry: connective tissue between functional components — more than A-to-B; done well, creates interest/anticipation as boundaries and spaces get progressively revealed
Character: material choices, site, sense of life beyond the aggregation of parts — related to elegance/emergence themes, applied to how a building feels over time
Magic: largely intangible, defined by the user’s experience (not designer/owner intent) — fosters delight and joyful appreciation of the unexpected

→ Present this six-part framework as genuinely different vocabulary from the process/operand, function/form language elsewhere in the course — captures dimensions (character, magic) that purely functional analysis leaves out

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.10 · Magic in Civil Architecture






Left: Sydney Opera House (a). Right: Golden Gate Bridge (b). Qualities of “Magic” allow structures to become memorable and iconic to a culture. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.10. Photos: (a) Wim Wiskerke/Alamy, (b) EvanTravels/Fotolia.



Sydney Opera House and Golden Gate Bridge — maximally recognizable examples of “magic”
Both are, at bottom, functional infrastructure (performance venues; a vehicular/pedestrian crossing) — yet both transcended pure function to become iconic symbols of their cities/countries — exactly the “magic” quality from the previous slide
→ Ask students for their own examples (buildings, bridges, everyday products) and push them to articulate why, using the six-part vocabulary, not a vague “it just looks cool.” Sets up the next slide’s deeper development of magic

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
On Magic



“Surprise, as all art and architecture, helps us contemplate. Life wears out our ability for surprise. Surprise is the beginning of a true vision of the world.” — Eladio Dieste




Magic is the emergence of elegance and character at the building level — the sleight of hand
It is difficult to define, but when something is magical, it’s immediately recognizable
Magic is the unusual circumstance that becomes normalized in good architecture — that moment of surprise that leaves a person in wonder and awe
Real magic makes architecture symbolic and iconic in a sustained manner — it reaches beyond the original intent, communicating viscerally with users



Eladio Dieste quote: surprise helps us contemplate — valuable because ordinary life, through repetition, wears out our capacity for surprise; a genuine architectural surprise is rare and valuable, “the beginning of a true vision of the world”
Progressively deeper definition of magic:

Magic = emergence of elegance and character at the building level (technical “emergence” sense, Ch. 2) — “the sleight of hand”
Difficult to define, but immediately recognizable when present — parallel to “you know it when you see it” properties, including elegance itself
The unusual circumstance that becomes normalized in good architecture — a moment of surprise leaving wonder/awe, not confusion
→ Real, lasting magic (not passing novelty) makes architecture symbolic/iconic in a sustained way — reaches beyond original designer intent, communicates viscerally with users regardless of whether they know that intent

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Figure 9.11 · Overlaying Performance and Poetry






A ballerina and a gymnast share athleticism, dynamic patterning, and nuance of expression — yet one is considered “art,” the other “athletic expertise.” An architect’s opportunity and responsibility: to overlay performance and poetry, and understand how those ingredients interact. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 9.11. Photos: (a) Cheese78/Fotolia, (b) Gerard Rancinan, Jean Guichard/Sygma/Corbis)



Closing comparison for the case study — unpack why it’s an apt final image
Ballerina and gymnast share athleticism, dynamic patterning, nuance of expression — yet one is culturally “art,” the other “athletic expertise” — a distinction of tradition/framing, not objective skill difference
Parallel to architecture: an architect’s opportunity/responsibility is to overlay performance (function, structural performance) and poetry (magic, character), and understand how they interact — not as separable concerns
→ Bridge back to the course: even though most of it focuses on analyzable concepts (form, function, decomposition, interfaces, goals), the actual practice of architecting has genuine room for elegance, character, and magic alongside engineering performance. Summary next returns to the analytical vocabulary

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Chapter 9 Summary

The architect is not a generalist, but a specialist in resolving ambiguity, focusing creativity, and simplifying complexity
Ambiguity comes in many forms — fuzziness, uncertainty, and missing, conflicting, or incorrect information — and the architect must recognize and deal with each
The architect is responsible for producing specific deliverables, central to reducing ambiguity and bridging corporate functions to the design environment
Product development processes differ superficially across firms and sectors, but share deep common structure — codified here as the Generic and Global PDPs
Architects must discern which segments of a PDP are centrally linked to their role, and stay skilled at interpreting new product development initiatives







Tip


Reference: Crawley, E., Cameron, B., & Selva, D. (2016). System Architecture: Strategy and Product Development for Complex Systems. Pearson. Chapter 9.





Walk the chapter’s full arc, tied to sections:

Opening: architect is not a generalist but a specialist — three roles: resolve ambiguity, employ creativity, manage complexity
Section 9.2: ambiguity’s precise forms — fuzziness + uncertainty (core), missing/conflicting/incorrect info ((X,Y,Z) shorthand) — plus the architect’s concrete deliverables (goals, context, concept, decomposition, interfaces, cost/schedule/risk)
Section 9.3: PDPs as an organizational ambiguity-management tool — four real-world PDPs (NASA, Helicopter Inc., Camera Co., Agile), differences sit atop deep common structure — Generic PDP (4 groups) → Global PDP (3 levels, W Questions)
Civil-architecture case study: architecting still has room for concept, character, magic

→ Closing practical charge: architects must discern which PDP segments are centrally linked to their role, and stay skilled at interpreting new development initiatives (Lean, Agile, Six Sigma, whatever’s next) on their actual merits, not fashion

title: The Role of the Architect
text:
Next: Up/Down-stream Influences
Chapter 10 examines the principal upstream and downstream influences on system architecture in detail — including the ABCD Product Case.


Close by pointing at Chapter 10, which this chapter has been setting up continuously
We’ve established, in the abstract, that the architect sits astride upstream influences (ambiguity flowing in) and downstream influences (ambiguity flowing back from design/implementation/operations)
Ch. 10 examines each category specifically and in depth: upstream (corporate strategy, marketing, regulation, technology infusion), downstream (implementation, operations, design-for-X, product evolution) — much deeper than this chapter’s compressed “Driving Ambiguity Out” list
→ Also introduces the ABCD (Architecture Business Case Decision) framework, for reasoning rigorously about how architectural choices connect to business outcomes — natural next step now that we know the architect’s role and how it fits the PDP

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
From Reverse to Forward Engineering

Chapters 4–6 pursued reverse engineering: the system already exists, so we analyzed its form, function, and architecture
Using centrifugal pumps and bubblesort to teach architecture was “a sledge hammer to a thumb tack” — simple systems don’t need the full toolkit
This chapter shifts to forward engineering: two new ideas, solution-neutral function and concept, plus two higher-complexity systems — an air transportation service and a home data network








Tip


Table 7.1 amends the Chapter 5 questions and adds a new one (7a) — collating everything into a method for synthesis, not just analysis.






Name the pivot: Chapters 4-6 = reverse engineering — system already exists, purely analytical (pump, bubblesort, bread slicing)
Book’s own memorable line, worth repeating verbatim: using simple systems like a pump/bubblesort to teach the full apparatus was “like taking a sledge hammer to a thumb tack” — but it let us learn the machinery without complexity in the way
Now two things at once: shift to forward engineering (nothing built yet, work toward a design), plus two new tools: solution-neutral function and concept
Two new running examples, chosen for realistic complexity: air transportation service (architecting applies to services, not just products) and home data network (“a microcosm of global information networking”)
→ Fragment previews Table 7.1: Chapter 5’s questions, amended, plus new Question 7a — one coherent method now supporting synthesis, not just analysis

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Box 7.1 · Principle of Solution-Neutral Function



“We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them.” — Albert Einstein




Poor system specifications frequently contain clues about an intended solution, function, or form — and those clues narrow the architect’s options before exploration even begins
Use solution-neutral functions where possible, and use the hierarchy of solution-neutral statements to scope how broad an exploration should be



First named principle — connect the Einstein quote to something concrete: specs that smuggle in a solution disguised as a requirement
Happens constantly, often invisibly: “add a corkscrew to the kitchen drawer inventory” already silently decided the solution before anyone asked the actual need (getting the cork out, or more broadly, accessing the wine)
→ Such a clue narrows exploration before it starts, foreclosing whole classes of alternatives (gas pressure, suction — next couple slides)
Prescription (have students repeat it back): state functions solution-neutrally — what, never how — and use the hierarchy of solution-neutral statements to scope how broad an exploration should be
→ Sets up the rest of the chapter as a rigorous methodology for exactly this

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Figure 7.1 · Concepts for Removing a Wine Bottle Cork
text:
Figure 7.1 · Concepts for Removing a Wine Bottle Cork



A corkscrew opens a wine bottle. But can we name other concepts for the same job?
We describe concepts as an operand-process-instrument set: cork (operand) pushing (process) injected gas (instrument)
Pulling alone is insufficient to describe a concept — “cork pulling with a screw” is a corkscrew









Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.1.



Chapter’s running worked example — simple, everyone has physical intuition, why the book leads with it
Everyone defaults to “corkscrew” — push further: how do you describe a corkscrew generally? Uses a screw to pull. Is pulling the only way?
Get creative: glue a tab and pull (no screw); create suction around the cork (real household product — hollow needle + hand pump); pressurize air inside the bottle, pushing the cork out; wine steward’s fork-like device that shears the cork’s sides off
Diagram = structured operand-process-instrument: operand always cork; process varies (pushing/shearing/pulling); each process has its own instruments (gas for pushing; fork/tube for shearing; suction/screw for pulling)
→ “Pulling” alone doesn’t specify a concept — need the instrument too. “Cork pulling with a screw” = corkscrew; pulling with suction is an entirely different concept sharing the same process

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Solution-Neutral Function in a Hierarchy

Drawing Figure 7.1 is itself a form of structured creativity (Ch. 12) — pulling led us to think about pushing, which we might otherwise have missed
Solution-neutral function exists in a hierarchy: translating the cork generalizes to removing the cork, which generalizes to opening the bottle, up to accessing the wine








Tip


The breadth of concepts we generate depends heavily on the functional intent we pose — the more solution-neutral the expression, the broader the set of concepts.






Meta-lesson from the previous slide: laying out Figure 7.1 systematically (rather than jumping to “corkscrew”) is itself a technique — formalized later (Ch. 12) as structured creativity
Starting from “pulling” and asking “what else could do this?” is precisely what surfaced “pushing” (gas) — nobody proposes that spontaneously
→ Structuring the concept space, even informally, surfaces options unstructured brainstorming misses
Second big idea: solution-neutral function forms a genuine hierarchy, not one fixed abstraction level — “translating the cork” → “removing the cork” → “opening the bottle” → “accessing the wine”; each step up trades specificity for breadth
→ Rule of thumb for the rest of the course: the more solution-neutral (higher up the hierarchy) the stated intent, the broader the resulting concept space — and the more work to explore it fully

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Figure 7.2 · A Hierarchy of Broader Concepts
text:
Figure 7.2 · A Hierarchy of Broader Concepts






Where to stop is a matter of practicality — with a wine bottle already on the table, concepts above “wine accessing” make no sense. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.2.



Walk top to bottom — concrete payoff of the previous slide’s abstract claim
Top: “accessing the wine” (most solution-neutral) → specializes down to “opening” the bottle, or “removing” the cork by “destroying” it (drilling, burning, melting — a different branch from “translating” the cork intact, which leads back to the corkscrew)
“Opening” further specializes into “breaching” the cork or “breaching” the bottle itself
Follow “translating” all the way down → lands exactly at “pushing/shearing/pulling” from Figure 7.1 — this diagram extends the previous one upward
→ Practicality: the architect always decides where in the hierarchy to stop — no formula, a judgment call. Wine bottle already on the table? Absurd to consider concepts above “wine accessing” (e.g. “beverage acquiring”) — the actual problem context constrains how far up is worth exploring

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Table 7.1 · Questions for Defining Concept







Question
Produces




7a. Who are the beneficiaries? What is the solution-neutral operand and its value-related attribute/process?
A solution-neutral framing of the desired function


5a. What is the value-related operand-process-form? What is the concept? What other concepts satisfy the same function?
The operand-process-form construct defining the system


5b. What are the internal functions? What are the concept fragments and integrated concept?
The internal processes/operands, first- and second-level





The chapter’s organizing scaffold — same numbering as Chapter 5’s question-based method (5a, 5b), amended with bracketed material, plus new Question 7a
→ Signals this chapter builds directly on Ch. 5-6, refining the same questions to now support forward, synthetic design work, not just backward analysis
7a (new, comes first): identify beneficiaries, derive solution-neutral operand + value-related attribute/process — the solution-neutral framing just practiced with wine-bottle
5a (amended): what’s the value-related operand-process-form? This is where concept gets defined — next major topic
5b (amended): internal functions, concept fragments, integrated concept — becomes Section 7.4
→ Treat this table as a running index: everything ahead answers one of these three questions in turn

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Deriving a Solution-Neutral Statement


The procedure (Question 7a):

Consider the beneficiary
Identify their need
Identify the solution-neutral operand that, acted upon, yields the benefit
Identify the operand’s attribute



Identify other relevant attributes of the operand
Define the solution-neutral process that changes the benefit-related attribute
Identify relevant attributes of that process









Tip


Two new examples: an air transportation service (beneficiary: the traveler) and a home data network (beneficiary: the surfer).






Concrete step-by-step procedure for Question 7a — an ordered checklist students can follow on future projects:

Consider who the beneficiary is (specific stakeholder, not abstract “the system”)
Identify their need in plain language
Crucial move: identify the solution-neutral operand — the thing that, acted upon, delivers the benefit (still abstract, not specific yet)
Identify the operand’s benefit-related attribute — the property whose change delivers value
Optionally, other relevant attributes of the operand
Define the solution-neutral process that changes that attribute (still abstract)
Optionally, attributes of that process

→ Two flagship worked examples for the rest of the lecture: air transportation service (beneficiary: traveler), home data network (beneficiary: surfer). Table 7.2 next works this exact procedure for both

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Table 7.2 · Formulating the Solution-Neutral Intent








Question
Transportation Service
Home Network




Beneficiary?
Traveler
Surfer


Need?
“Visit a client in another city”
“Buy a cool book”


Solution-neutral operand?
Traveler
Book


Benefit-related attribute?
Location
Ownership


Other operand attributes?
Alone with light luggage
Consistent with tastes


Solution-neutral process?
Changing (transporting)
Buying


Attributes of process?
Safely and on demand
Online





Walk both columns carefully — pause on why the operand choice takes real thought, not obvious at first glance
Transportation: beneficiary = traveler, need = “visit a client in another city” (conceptually rich: going, spending time, returning). Solution-neutral operand = the traveler themselves (not “trip” or “distance”). Benefit-related attribute = location. Other attributes: alone, light luggage. Process = “changing”/“transporting,” attributes: safely, on demand
→ Full statement (have students say aloud): “safely and on demand transporting to a new location a traveler with light luggage” — nothing says how — still entirely solution-neutral
Home network: beneficiary = surfer, need = “buy a cool book.” Operand = the book; attribute = ownership; other attribute = consistent with tastes. Process = buying, attribute = online
→ Combined: “buying online a book that the buyer likes” — again no how yet
These two statements become the functional intent driving both worked examples for the rest of the chapter

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Intent Vanishes When the System Operates
text:
Intent Vanishes When the System Operates



When a system operates, the intent vanishes. Watching a room full of servers, or a plane in flight, it’s hard to tell why — the architect must record intent, because once built, the system rarely says it back.




In summary: the functional intent for a system should be stated as a solution-neutral function — an operand and a process (with their attributes) linked to value, containing no reference to solution.



Sobering, practical point — easy to underestimate until seen: once a system operates, its intent becomes invisible
Can’t look at a room of running servers and read off why they exist. Can’t look at a plane in flight and recover the stakeholder need
Book’s observation: intent is normally handled casually in real orgs — hallway conversations (“I thought we were building a retro-inspired minivan”), loose concept art, rarely written down rigorously
→ This is why this chapter’s formalism matters (even if pedantic at first): the architect must record intent, because reconstructing it later from the finished system can be genuinely difficult or impossible
Core rule, worth writing down verbatim: functional intent = solution-neutral function — operand + process + attributes, linked to value, no reference to solution

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
The Notion of Concept

The intellectual distance from solution-neutral function to architecture is a large gap to jump — concept bridges it
Concept is the transition point from solution-neutral to solution-specific
It must allow value-related functions to be executed, enabled by form; it establishes the vocabulary for the solution; it implicitly sets design parameters and the level of technology



Motivate why this section exists: a clean solution-neutral statement (Section 7.2) is necessary, but it’s still an enormous leap to a full detailed architecture (Ch. 6/8) — too large to jump in one step
Concept bridges that gap — not strictly necessary logically, but enormously useful practically as a tractable intermediate stopping point
Three defining properties:

Transition point where thinking shifts from solution-neutral to solution-specific
Must allow the value-related function to be executed, enabled by some (still abstracted) form
Establishes vocabulary for the rest of the design process; implicitly sets design parameters and level of technology

→ We’ll see the vocabulary-setting effect concretely on “Concept, Concretely” coming up

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Box 7.2 · Definition of Concept



Concept is a product or system vision, idea, notion, or mental image that maps function to form. It embodies a sense of how the system will function and an abstraction of the system form — a simplification of the architecture that allows for high-level reasoning.




Concept is not a system attribute, but a notional mapping between two attributes: form and function.



Unpack the formal definition phrase by phrase — every word doing real work
Concept is a vision — deliberately evocative, human language, not a rigorous engineering spec
It’s a mapping of function to form — same kind of mapping full architecture eventually captures, just coarser resolution
Embodies a sense of function and an abstraction of form → a simplification of the full architecture, tractable enough to reason about at a high level
→ Ontological distinction (pause on this): concept is not an attribute of the system (not a “thing it has,” like mass or color) — it’s a notional mapping connecting the form attribute and the function attribute. Lives at the level of how we’re choosing to relate them, not as a standalone property

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Figure 7.3 · Concept and Architecture






Concept and architecture both map function to form — concept does it in a general way, architecture in elaborate detail. If you have a concept, it guides the architecture; if you have an architecture, concept rationalizes it. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.3.



Two panels, direct visual statement: left = concept, a coarse general arrow in a simple form-vs-function grid; right = architecture, same grid but filled with a dense fine-grained matrix — elaborate, high-resolution version of the same mapping
Two-way relationship, both useful in practice:

Forward (synthesis): concept as a guide, constraining how you build out the full architecture — most of this chapter and the next
Backward (analysis, Ch. 4-6’s practice): concept rationalizes an existing architecture — compresses overwhelming detail into one comprehensible high-level story

→ Both directions matter; good architects move fluidly between them

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Concept, Concretely







Tip


Pump: solution-neutral function is “moving fluid.” The concept is water (specific operand), pressurizing (specific process), using a centrifugal pump (specific instrument of form).











Tip


Bubblesort is literally the name of a concept: array (specific operand: entries), sequentially exchanging (specific process), using bubblesort (specific instrument).





Naming the specific instrument (centrifugal pump, bubblesort) immediately establishes a vocabulary, sets design parameters, and implies a level of technology



Ground the abstract definition in the two examples students know cold from Ch. 4-6 — makes “concept sets vocabulary” concrete, not just asserted
Pump: solution-neutral function = “moving fluid” (says nothing about what fluid or how). Concept specializes: operand → water, process → pressurizing, instrument → centrifugal pump
→ Naming “centrifugal pump” supplies, for free: a technical vocabulary (motor, housing, impeller), concrete design parameters (impeller speed, pressure rise), and an implied level of technology (above buckets, below jet-engine turbomachinery)
Bubblesort makes the point even sharper — the name is literally the concept. Solution-neutral function = “sorting the array” → specific operand (array entries), process (sequentially exchanging), instrument (the bubblesort algorithm itself)
→ Just saying “bubblesort” conjures a complete vocabulary, mechanism, and instrument set (down to the code). Contrast with how little is pinned down before the concept is chosen — choosing a concept commits an enormous amount of information all at once

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Figure 7.4 · Template for Deriving Concept






Five key ideas (thick borders): solution-neutral operand, specific operand, specific system operating, generic concept form, specific system form. Intent → Function → Form. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.4.



Three-column structure, left to right — formalizes everything so far into a repeatable procedure
Intent (left): solution-neutral operand, sitting outside the dashed “Concept” boundary — the precursor, not itself part of the concept
Function (middle): specific operand + specific operating process — where the solution-neutral operand gets specialized (specialization-triangle relationship, echoes OPM notation from Ch. 3)
Form (right): specific instrument of form, connected to the process it enables
Five highlighted shapes to name from memory: solution-neutral operand, specific operand, specific system operating, generic concept form, specific system form
Reconnect to examples: pump — “moving fluid” → water (operand) → pressurizing (operating) → centrifugal pump (form). Bubblesort — array (solution-neutral) → array entries → sequentially exchanging → bubblesort (form, not quicksort)
→ This is the operational procedure to use whenever deriving a concept from solution-neutral intent in project work

There is no single relationship between solution-neutral and specific operand/process — specializing to concept requires creativity, not automation.



Comparative capstone — same template applied across all five running examples from Ch. 4-7, side by side
Quick pattern reinforcement: fluid/moving → water/pressurizing (centrifugal pump); array/sorting → array-entries/sequentially-exchanging (bubblesort); cork/translating → cork/pulling (screw); traveler/transporting → traveler/flying (airplane); book/buying → internet/accessing (home DSL)
Key teaching point (side-caption, dwell on it): no single consistent relationship between solution-neutral and specific operand. Sometimes identical (cork stays cork), sometimes totally different (book → internet)
→ Foreshadows Box 7.3’s catalog of specialization patterns. Lesson: specializing to concept is not mechanical — requires real creativity and judgment, no shortcut formula

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Box 7.3 · Specializing Function to Concept
A few of the patterns the specific operand can take, relative to the solution-neutral operand:

Completely different operand and process: entertaining a person by watching a DVD
Same process, different operand: choosing a leader by choosing the president
Part of the solution-neutral operand: opening the bottle by removing the cork
A type of the solution-neutral operand: moving fluid by pressurizing water
An attribute of the solution-neutral operand: amplifying a signal by increasing signal voltage








Tip


Similar patterns apply to specializing the process — e.g., transporting a traveler by flying a traveler.






Cashes out the previous slide’s observation — catalog of the patterns that can occur, so students have a checklist rather than specializing haphazardly
Completely different: entertaining a person → watching a DVD (neither word appears in the original)
Same process, different operand: choosing a leader → choosing the president
Part of the solution-neutral operand: opening the bottle → removing the cork (cork is part of the bottle)
A type of the solution-neutral operand: moving fluid → pressurizing water (water is a type of fluid — the class/specialization relationship from Ch. 3, now applied to concepts)
An attribute of the solution-neutral operand: amplifying a signal → increasing signal voltage
→ Same variety of patterns recurs when specializing the process instead, holding operand fixed: transporting a traveler → flying a traveler (“traveler” unchanged, only the verb changes)
Encourage students, in their own project work, to check their concept against this catalog: which pattern does it follow, and would a different pattern reveal concepts they hadn’t considered?

Direct continuation of Table 7.2 (which stopped at solution-neutral function) — push both examples through the Figure 7.4 template to a fully specified concept
Transportation: specific operand stays “traveler” (“same as solution-neutral” pattern), attribute “location,” other attributes “alone, light luggage.” Process specializes to “flying,” attribute “in less than 2 hours.” Generic “dummy form” placeholder “Flyer” → specific form “airplane,” attribute “commercial”
→ Plain language: “a single traveler with light luggage, flying in less than two hours, using a commercial airplane”

→ Plain language: “reliably accessing a high-speed internet connection using an inexpensive home DSL network”
Have students say both sentences aloud — reads almost like natural language (Chomsky noun-verb-noun parallel from Ch. 2)

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Naming Concepts

No simple convention exists — rationally, concepts are named operand + process + instrument, as in light + emitting + diode
Naming for just the operand rarely works — a “mower” only makes sense because of the implicit “er” ending suggesting an instrument
Sometimes a concept is named for an attribute: “wireless” described two entirely different concepts, a century apart








Tip


Developing concepts is an open-ended creative process — the architect should build a rich set of alternatives before sorting and down-selecting (Ch. 11).






Honest, practical note: no single simple naming convention — but rationally, systematic naming = operand + process + instrument
LED = the book’s cleanest real example: light (operand) + emitting (process) + diode (instrument), all three legible in the name
Linguistic subtlety: naming by operand alone rarely works (“grass” means nothing as a device name) — English implicitly appends “-er” to imply the missing process/instrument. “Mower” works because “-er” is parsed as “a thing that does the mowing,” even though “mow” and the actual mechanism stay unstated
“Wireless” story: same word named two completely different concepts a century apart — early 1900s = radio broadcasting (literally no wires), early 2000s = local data networking (Wi-Fi)
→ Naming aside, developing concepts is open-ended and creative — build a rich set of alternatives before sorting/down-selecting (deferred to Ch. 11’s formal stakeholder-driven criteria)

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Figure 7.5 · A Tree of Concept Options
text:
Figure 7.5 · A Tree of Concept Options






An operand layer, a process layer, and an instrumental form layer. Fewer operand options than process options, and fewer process options than form options — a decision tree. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.5.



General template for organizing concept alternatives — next several slides apply it to each running example
Three layers: operand (top), process (middle, several operating options can branch off one operand), instrumental form (bottom, several form options can branch off each process)
→ Predictable tree shape: fewer operand options than process options, fewer process options than form options — tree widens going down (many physical/technological ways to implement a given operating principle, fewer fundamentally different operating principles per operand)
Connects back to Section 7.1’s wine-cork example (pushing/shearing/pulling generated deliberately, not jumping to corkscrew) — this tree is the general-purpose tool for that same structured alternative-generation, applied next to pump, bubblesort, transportation, home network

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Figure 7.6 · Pump Concept Options






Seven non-exhaustive concept options for moving fluid — from pressurizing with a centrifugal pump, to blowing air with a fan. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.6.



Apply the decision-tree template to the pump — from “fluid”/“moving,” branches by specific operand: water vs. air
Water: pressurizing (centrifugal or axial-flow pump), accelerating (a different centrifugal pump, or jet ejector), displacing (rotary or reciprocating displacement pump)
Air: blowing (fan)
→ Seven distinct concept options total, explicitly non-exhaustive
Notice: centrifugal pump appears twice (under pressurizing and accelerating) — same instrument, two different operating principles. Instrument, process, operand are three separable choices, not one bundled decision
→ Concept space for “moving fluid” is much richer than the default answer (“get a pump”) without structured exploration

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Figure 7.7 · Bubblesort Concept Options






Three principles of operation for sorting an array — sequentially exchanging, inserting, displacing — each with specific algorithms. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.7.



Same template applied to sorting — “array”/“sorting,” array entries as the operand throughout, three operating principles:

Sequentially exchanging — bubblesort, or cocktail sort
Inserting — insertion sort, or shell sort
Displacing — partitioning algorithm, notably quicksort

Satisfying for students with programming background — sorting algorithms they know, now organized as principles + instruments
→ Quicksort (often taught as just “a fast algorithm”) sits under a genuinely different operating principle than bubblesort/insertion sort — reinforces the pump lesson: concept options aren’t just different implementations of the same idea, some represent fundamentally different operating principles the architect must recognize before comparing fairly

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Figure 7.8 · Transportation Concept Options






Flying, rolling, and floating — each linked to common instruments. Traveler is the only likely operand; transporting is a long-standing human endeavor. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.8.



Template applied to the transportation service — scaling up real-world complexity from pump/sorting
Specific operand barely branches (traveler is really the only sensible one) — process branches into three long-standing strategies: flying (airplane, helicopter), rolling (car, train), floating (boat, e.g. sailboat)
→ Unlike pump/sorting (modern, narrow engineering problems), transporting is “a long-standing human endeavor” — millennia of technologies; the book limits the tree to these three for tractability, not exhaustiveness
Ask students what’s missing (walking, tunneling, space travel) — reinforces that “non-exhaustive” is a real constraint the architect must accept

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Figure 7.9 · Home Network Concept Options






A far more limited option space — buying a book online basically requires accessing the Internet, so the only real options are how you access it. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.9.



Template applied to the home network — useful contrast: this tree is genuinely narrower, ask students to articulate why
Operand (“Internet”) and process (“accessing”) barely branch — no way around needing internet access to buy a book online. Only the instrument branches: home DSL, home cable, mobile broadband, public WiFi, work cable
→ Not every solution-neutral function generates an equally rich alternative space — sometimes it collapses to “same basic approach, instrument varies.” A legitimate, useful outcome, not a failure — recognizing a narrow solution space is itself valuable architectural insight, telling the architect where creative effort will and won’t pay off

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Broader Concepts and Hierarchy

The concept-option analysis looked “downward” toward increasing detail — but we can also look “upward” toward increasingly general intent
Why move fluid? Maybe to dry a basement. Why dry a basement? Maybe to improve living conditions
There is hierarchy in functional intent, just as there is hierarchy in built systems





The specific function at one level becomes the solution-neutral functional intent at the next level down.






Pivot — echoes the wine-bottle “upward vs. downward” move (Figures 7.1-7.2), now generalized to all four examples
Figures 7.5-7.9 explored downward. Upward questions: why move fluid? Maybe to dry a basement. Why dry a basement? Maybe to improve living conditions
→ Just as built systems have hierarchy (Ch. 3), functional intent has hierarchy too — no reason the level you first stated is the “true” one, it’s just wherever the conversation started
Single most important insight, write on the board: the specific function at one level becomes the solution-neutral intent at the next level down — a precise, recursive relationship
→ Means the Section 7.2/7.3 procedure chains downward through as many levels as useful, each level’s output concept becoming the next level’s input. Next two slides (7.10, 7.11) show this chaining worked out for both examples

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Figure 7.10 · A Hierarchy Leading to Flying the Traveler
text:
Figure 7.10 · A Hierarchy Leading to Flying the Traveler


Closing a deal, by learning client preferences, by meeting the client, by traveling, by flying. At every level there are alternatives — a teleconference instead of a visit, a train instead of a flight. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.10.



Worked demonstration of the recursive relationship, top to bottom: “closing a deal” (ultimate reason) → “learning client preferences” → “meeting the client” → “traveling” → “flying” (matches Table 7.4)
Practically useful part (side-caption): at every level, real alternatives exist that a narrower fixed-level analysis would never surface
Instead of meeting to learn preferences: study published materials, attend a conference. Instead of traveling at all: a tele-meeting, skipping “traveling” entirely. Instead of flying: drive or train
→ No single objectively “right” level to start at — but understanding intent’s hierarchy going up reveals entirely different solution categories (teleconference instead of any physical travel)

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Figure 7.11 · A Hierarchy Leading to Home Internet Access
text:
Figure 7.11 · A Hierarchy Leading to Home Internet Access


Entertainment → reading books → buying books → buying online → accessing the network. Understanding this hierarchy might surface new options, like selling electronic books. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.11.



Second hierarchy, equal treatment: “entertaining” (broadest) → “reading” (sibling alternatives: listening, viewing) → “buying” a book (sibling: borrowing) → “buying online” (sibling: physical store, call center) → “accessing” the network (chapter’s working level)
Practical payoff, worth real time: understanding the hierarchy surfaces new business options a narrower analysis would miss — book calls out “selling electronic books”
→ Selling ebooks doesn’t require buying (traditional sense) or the same home network connection — emerges only by stepping back up to “reading” and re-asking “what other ways could this need be met?”
Good closer for the whole first half of the chapter: stating things solution-neutrally and understanding intent’s full hierarchy isn’t pedantry — it’s a concrete tool for finding otherwise-invisible business/design opportunities

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Section 7.3 Summary

Concept is a system vision that maps function to form; it sets the solution vocabulary and design parameters, and rationalizes the architecture
Concept is derived by specializing the solution-neutral operand and process to a specific operand, process, and abstraction of form
There is no naming convention, and no single relationship between solution-neutral and specific — concept generation requires creativity
Concepts sit in a hierarchy: understanding it one or two levels up is very useful for the architect



Checkpoint before Section 7.4 — students should be comfortable with:

The formal definition of concept and why it’s a useful intermediate step
Walking the Figure 7.4 template on a system of their choosing
No single fixed specialization pattern (Box 7.3) — requires creative judgment, not mechanical rules
Concepts form a hierarchy — looking one or two levels up can surface categorically different options (Figures 7.10, 7.11)

→ Closes Section 7.3’s “what a concept is and how to derive one.” Next: what happens when a concept’s process is rich enough to unpack into several internal sub-processes?

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Rich Concepts and Concept Fragments

A concept’s process is often rich in meaning, and can be “unpacked” into several internal functions — visiting a client implies going there, spending time, and returning
An integrated concept is made of smaller concept fragments — one per internal process — combined recursively using the same concept-development procedure








Tip


Transporting has at least three important internal processes: lifting (overcoming gravity), propelling (overcoming drag), and guiding. Without all three, transporting doesn’t work.






Section 7.4’s central new idea — recall “visiting a client” was called “conceptually rich” (going, spending time, returning). That richness is what this section formalizes
A concept’s process can be unpacked into several distinct internal functions that must all happen for it to work
Define precisely: an integrated concept is built from smaller concept fragments, one per unpacked internal process — each developed with the same operand-process-instrument procedure, applied recursively (callback to Ch. 3’s recursion)
Primary worked example: “transporting” has at least three necessary internal processes — lifting (overcoming gravity), propelling (overcoming drag), guiding
→ Emphasize “necessary”: without all three, transporting doesn’t work as a concept (can’t have a vehicle that overcomes gravity/drag with no way to steer). Sets up the morphological-matrix analysis next

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
The Morphological Matrix

For a car, lifting, propelling, and guiding are all done by wheels — a car is wheels-wheels-wheels
A train differs only in guiding — wheels-wheels-ground
Combining one instrument per internal process across many choices reveals a surprising number of integrated concepts — this structured layout is a morphological matrix (covered in full in Ch. 14)



“Wheels-wheels-wheels” — memorable shorthand for compressing a vehicle’s whole architecture into three words
Car: lifting, propelling, guiding all done by the wheels — lift (support weight), propel (friction + engine), guide (steering)
Train differs in exactly one process: lifting/propelling still wheels, but guiding = rail/ground itself (rails constrain the path, no active steering) → wheels-wheels-ground
→ Striking: cars and trains feel like completely different vehicle categories but differ conceptually in exactly one instrument choice out of three
Morphological matrix: one row per internal process, one column per instrument choice per row — combine systematically to enumerate integrated concepts, not by ad hoc guessing
(Flag: full treatment comes in Ch. 14 — here, just the basic idea and payoff)

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Table 7.6 · Morphological Matrix for Transporting






Each column is an integrated concept. Aircraft and gliders differ only in propulsion; airships and submarines are conceptually identical, differing only in operating medium. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Table 7.6.



Table structure: three rows (lifting, propelling, guiding), each with several instrument options (wheels, propeller, wings, hull for lifting; wheels, propeller, jet, gravity for propelling; wheels, propeller, rudder, “ground” for guiding). Eleven columns = eleven integrated vehicle concepts (car, train, jet aircraft, propeller aircraft, helicopter, airship, glider, boat, submarine, jet boat, hydrofoil), each an X-pattern across the rows
Two illuminating comparisons (side-caption):

Aircraft and gliders: same lifting (wings), same guiding (rudder), differ in exactly one row — propelling (propeller vs. gravity). A glider = “an aircraft with the propulsion instrument removed”
Airships and submarines: conceptually identical across all three processes, differing only in operating medium (air vs. water) — most people would never draw this comparison, but the underlying morphology matches

→ Exactly the kind of unexpected structural insight a systematic morphological matrix surfaces that ad hoc brainstorming misses

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
text:
Integrating the Home Data Network

The home network has five key internal processes: connecting the local network to the ISP; modulating the ISP carrier signal; managing data on the local network; connecting user devices; interacting with the user
Combining one instrument per process (with some flexibility — a residential gateway and a separate WAP can both manage the network) yields an integrated concept



Same methodology, second example, equal depth: “accessing” unpacks into five internal processes — have students explain each:

Connecting the local network to the ISP (the “last mile”)
Modulating the ISP’s carrier signal (a modem’s job)
Managing data on the local network (a gateway/router’s job)
Connecting user devices (WiFi, Ethernet)
Interacting with the user (laptop, phone, etc.)

→ Useful nuance beyond car/train: real integrated concepts have more flexibility than exactly one instrument per process — a single device might combine rows (gateway doing modulation and management), or a function might split across devices (gateway and a separate WAP both managing data)
Flag honestly: morphological matrices are powerful but don’t always map with perfectly clean one-instrument-per-row simplicity — the architect uses judgment on how strictly to apply the framework

title: Solution-Neutral Function and Concepts
section: Figure 7.12 · An Integrated Concept for the Home Network
text:
Figure 7.12 · An Integrated Concept for the Home Network






A DSL modem plus a box combining a residential gateway and Ethernet switch, with both WiFi and Ethernet connections to user devices. Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 7.12.



One concrete, fully-specified integrated concept — trace the signal path left to right
ISP side (broadband remote access server, DSLAM at the exchange) → phone line → DSL modem in the home → integrated box (residential gateway + Ethernet switch) → wired Ethernet to desktop PC and printer; separate WAP gives WiFi to laptop and cell phone
→ This is “Integrated Concept 1” from the upcoming Table 7.8: DSL (connect to ISP), dedicated DSL modem (modulate), gateway+switch+WAP (manage data), WiFi+Ethernet (connect devices), laptop/phone/desktop/printer (user interaction)
Good template for students’ own diagrams — much more concrete/buildable than earlier purely functional OPM diagrams, because every box is a specific instrument, not a solution-neutral placeholder

text:
